My issues are much more about struggling to stay focused, getting easily distracted, and feeling physically restless or antsy. My main struggles are much more about staying focused and getting organized, rather than being impulsive in conversations.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations where you might have acted on impulse, such as making reckless decisions or engaging in impulsive behaviors, outside of your difficulties with focus and restlessness?\n\nPatient: I can't really think of any times where I've acted impulsively or made reckless decisions. My issues are much more about struggling to stay focused, getting easily distracted, and feeling physically restless or antsy. I've never really been someone who acts on impulse like that.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood but worsened with your job change; can you describe how your symptoms impact your daily life and relationships outside of work, such as with friends and family?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed my symptoms affecting my relationships with friends or family too much. Most of my struggles and stress are concentrated on my work and keeping up with daily tasks like remembering appointments, rather than my social life.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when you had to engage in activities that required sustained mental effort, like studying for a test or working on a complex project, and how you managed your focus and restlessness during those times?\n\nPatient: In school and college, I managed by cramming right before exams and relying on my memory, but now I hit a \"mental wall\" with long files and avoid them by checking email or getting coffee. To deal with the restlessness during those long tasks, I constantly bounce my leg, click my pen, or get up to grab water during meetings just to move around.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when you felt like you were able to focus and avoid distractions, but still experienced significant restlessness or fidgeting, or was it usually the case that when you were able to focus, the restlessness decreased?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure or haven't paid close enough attention to whether the fidgeting goes away on the rare occasions I can actually focus. But when I'm at my desk trying to get through my files, the leg bouncing and pen clicking seem to happen constantly anyway.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances where you exhibited excessive running, climbing, or other physical activity in inappropriate situations, such as in a quiet office setting or during a meeting?\n\nPatient: I don't recall ever doing things like running or climbing in inappropriate situations. I do get really antsy and fidgety at my desk, or feel the need to get up and walk around, but it has never been anything extreme like that.\n\nDoctor: You've described significant difficulties with focus and restlessness, but can you clarify if you've ever experienced a period where your symptoms of inattention were more prominent than your restlessness, or vice versa, to help understand the balance between these issues?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure if there were ever distinct periods where one was worse than the other. The focus and daydreaming issues have felt pretty constant since childhood, while the restlessness and fidgeting are things I mostly notice when I'm forced to sit still at my desk for a long time. I don't really think of them as separate phases.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with inattention, such as daydreaming and struggling to focus, have always been a more significant problem for you than your restlessness and fidgeting, or have there been times when the restlessness was the more dominant issue?\n\nPatient: Yes, the daydreaming and focus problems have definitely always been the much bigger and more dominant issue for me, dating all the way back to elementary school. While I do get restless and fidget at my desk, those physical symptoms have never been nearly as disruptive as my mental struggles with focusing, organizing, and actually getting my work done.\n\nDoctor: To confirm, you feel that your difficulties with focus and attention have always been the primary issue for you, rather than the restlessness and fidgeting, which have been more of a secondary concern, is that correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that's absolutely correct.
